transcript.text: My indesit washing machine fills with water and drains but the drum just doesn't go round at all. Its an IWC something. Had it about 9 years. Is it worth fixing?

Probably yes, if it's one of the common cheap faults. On Indesit IWC machines, a drum that won't turn while everything else works usually comes down to a few things, and the most likely ones are cheap.

## Most likely causes (roughly in order)

1. Worn carbon brushes in the motor. This is very common on Indesits around 8 to 10 years old. The brushes wear down until the motor stops getting power. Parts cost about £10–20.
2. Drive belt snapped or slipped off. Parts cost about £10–15, and it's an easy fix.
3. Something jammed between the drum and tub, like an underwire, coin or sock. Free to fix if you can get it out.
4. Faulty motor, around £60–120 for the part.
5. Faulty control board (PCB), around £60–150. This is the one that usually makes repair not worth it.

## Quick checks you can do (unplug it first)

• Turn the drum by hand (empty, door open):
• It spins really freely and easily: the belt has probably come off or snapped.
• It feels stiff, stuck or grinds: something may be jammed, or the bearings are going (often there's loud rumbling on spin beforehand).
• It turns normally with a bit of resistance: the belt is likely fine, so suspect brushes, motor or board.
• Listen during a wash. If it fills but there's no hum or attempt from the motor, that points to brushes, motor or board. If you hear the motor whirring but the drum isn't moving, that's the belt.
• Look for flashing lights. Indesits flash error codes on the panel. Note which lights flash and how many times, and you can look up the code for your model.
• Check the model number. It's on the sticker inside the door rim, e.g. IWC 71252 or similar. You'll need it for ordering parts.

To check the belt and brushes, you take the back panel off (a few screws). The belt is right there, and the brushes are on the motor at the bottom.

## Is it worth it?

| Fault | DIY cost | With engineer | Worth it? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Belt | ~£15 | ~£80–120 | Yes |
| Carbon brushes | ~£15–20 | ~£90–130 | Yes |
| Motor | ~£60–120 | ~£150–200 | Borderline |
| PCB | ~£60–150 | ~£150–250 | Probably not |
| Drum bearings | ~£30 (but a big job) | £150+ | Usually not on an Indesit |

A basic new washing machine is roughly £250–350. At 9 years old, I'd say fix it if it's the belt or brushes (especially if you're happy to DIY), and think about replacing it if it's the board, motor or bearings.

If you tell me the full model number and what happens when you turn the drum by hand, I can help narrow it down further.

Thanks. I've looked at the label inside the door and it reads IWC 71252. With the power off the drum turns freely and quietly by hand, no scraping or rumble. I'll take the back panel off and look at the belt and brushes next, unless you'd suggest otherwise.

That's the right next step. A drum that turns quietly with no grinding rules out a jam or failing bearings, so it's down to the belt, brushes, motor or board.

Is the belt still on?
"Freely" can mean two things:
• Belt off or snapped: the drum spins very easily and keeps going for a moment when you let go.
• Belt on: there's slight resistance, and if you listen closely you may hear the motor turning with it.

The back panel will settle it either way.

## Taking the back panel off

1. Unplug it, then pull the machine out far enough to work behind it.
2. Undo the screws around the edge of the back panel (usually Phillips or Torx) and lift it away.

## What to check

Belt (the large pulley at the top, belt running down to the motor)
• Is it on both pulleys?
• Is it cracked, shredded, glazed or loose? It should feel fairly tight when you press it.
• If it's simply come off, it can usually be refitted. Loop it over the motor pulley first, then onto the drum pulley, and turn the drum by hand so it rolls on. If it's stretched or damaged, replace it. It slipped off for a reason.

Carbon brushes (on the motor at the bottom, one on each side)
• Each sits in a small plastic holder held by a screw or clip, with a wire attached. Take a photo before disconnecting anything.
• New brushes are roughly 30–35 mm long. If they're down to about 10 mm or less, or chipped or cracked, they need replacing. Always replace both as a pair.
• Brush wear is a very common cause of exactly your symptoms on an Indesit this age.

While you're there
• Look at the wiring plug on the motor. Is it pushed fully home, with no scorching or melted plastic?
• If you can see the copper commutator (where the brushes touch), check for deep grooves or burnt sections. That would point to the motor itself.

## Ordering parts

Search by your model, IWC 71252, to get the right belt or brushes. Check the motor's own label too, as Indesit used more than one motor maker and the brushes differ.

## If belt and brushes are both fine

Then it's the motor or the control board. Before going further, watch the panel during a wash for flashing lights and note the pattern, since it can point to which one.

Rough repair costs, to finish the table from before:

| Fault | DIY cost | With engineer | Worth it? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Belt | ~£15 | ~£80–120 | Yes |
| Carbon brushes | ~£15–20 | ~£90–130 | Yes |
| Motor | ~£60–120 | ~£150–220 | Borderline |
| Control board | ~£60–150 | ~£150–250 | Usually not at 9 years |

Let me know what you find and I can help with the next step.

I've had the back panel off. The belt is on both pulleys and feels tight. I also took the two carbon brushes out: one is very short and blackened at the tip, the other is a bit longer. Does that sound like the cause?

Yes, that's very likely the cause. One brush worn very short with a blackened tip fits your symptoms exactly: once a brush gets too short it stops making proper contact, the motor gets no power, and everything else (filling, draining) carries on as normal. Uneven wear between the two is common.

## What to do

Replace both brushes as a pair, even though one looks better. Mixing old and new causes uneven contact and the old one won't be far behind.

Before ordering, check the motor label. It's on the motor casing, and the maker is often Welling, Sole, Ceset or Nidec. Brushes differ between makers, so match the brushes to the motor as well as the model number (IWC 71252). Take a photo of the old brushes and holders to compare against listings. Expect about £10–20 for a pair.

Check the commutator while the brushes are out. Turn the drum slowly by hand and look through the brush openings at the copper segments:
• Smooth, evenly darkened copper is normal and fine.
• Deep grooves, pitting, burnt or missing segments, or a heavy buildup of black dust mean the motor itself may be damaged, and new brushes might not last long.

A light layer of carbon dust is normal; you can gently blow or brush it out.

## Fitting the new brushes

1. Fit each brush into its holder the same way round as the old one. The curved face of the brush should sit against the commutator.
2. Make sure the brush slides freely in the holder and the spring presses it firmly on.
3. Reconnect the wires exactly as in your photo and check the motor plug is pushed fully home.
4. Refit the back panel before plugging back in.

## After fitting

• Run a short empty wash first. New brushes need to "bed in" to the shape of the commutator, so you may see a few sparks, smell a slight burning odour or get a bit less power for the first couple of washes. That's normal and should settle.
• If it's still sparking heavily or smelling after a few washes, that points back to the commutator or motor.

## If the drum still doesn't turn

The next suspects would be the motor itself (a winding fault) or the control board. At that point, with a 9-year-old machine, it's worth weighing up a motor replacement against a new washer. But given what you've found, there's a good chance a £15 pair of brushes gets it working again.

That sounds plausible, thank you. One thing I should have mentioned: a few weeks ago I noticed a faint hot electrical smell near the machine, though not since. Does that change anything, or is it just the worn brush?

Most likely it's the same fault. A brush wearing down loses spring pressure and contact, so it starts arcing (sparking) against the commutator. That produces exactly that hot electrical smell, and the blackened tip on your short brush is the sign of it. The smell then stopping fits too: once the brush got too short to make contact, the motor stopped running, so there was nothing left to arc.

Because heavy arcing can do some collateral damage, take a few extra minutes to check these while the back is off.

## Extra checks before fitting new brushes

Commutator (most important)
• Look for burnt or blackened patches, pitting, grooves or raised/lifted copper segments.
• Heavy arcing can damage it. If it's badly marked, new brushes may spark, smell and wear out quickly, and the motor may need replacing instead.

Brush holders and wiring
• Check the plastic brush holders for melting or scorching.
• Check the brush wires and their terminals for discolouration or brittle insulation.

Motor connector
• Unplug the motor's wiring block and look at the pins and plastic for browning, melting or burnt pins. A loose connection here can also cause a hot smell.

Other places worth a glance
• Mains plug and socket: any discolouration, or does the plug get warm in use? A failing socket or plug is a genuine fire risk and worth ruling out.
• Heater connections: at the front or back, low down on the tub. Check for scorched terminals.

## After the repair

• A slight smell during the first wash or two while the new brushes bed in is normal.
• If you get a strong or persistent burning smell, see smoke, or the smell is coming from somewhere other than the motor area, stop the machine, unplug it, and investigate before using it again.
• Don't leave it running unattended for the first few washes.

If everything looks clean apart from the worn brush, you can be fairly confident the smell was just the brush arcing and the new pair should sort it.
